The proposed epoch tagging calls for treating acknowledgments according to the epoch they identify. An older acknowledgment alone does not establish the status of a certificate for the new epoch. If the implementation wants to reuse any conclusion, it would need a sound justification for its applicability to the new sealed edge set; the proposal does not define such a reuse rule.
Does tagging tell us which shards need to acknowledge an invalidation?

No. It says how to associate an acknowledgment with an epoch, not which invalidations exist or whose acknowledgment is required. The proposal leaves the discovery and coordination rules unspecified. Those rules would have to be sound wherever an affected SCC depends on information across shards.
What does quiescence mean at this point in the sequence?

It means the distributed work relevant to preparing that epoch’s result has settled: no outstanding work that the quiescence condition covers can still change the candidate answer. A worker’s empty local queue alone would not establish global quiescence if work remains elsewhere or in transit. The proposal names the condition but does not define its detection protocol.
If quiescence is established, why validate certificates afterward?

Because completion of maintenance work does not independently establish that its structural assumptions are sound for the sealed edge set. Post-quiescence validation checks affected-SCC certificates after that work has settled, before allowing the resulting epoch to be published. It is an additional validity check, not another name for quiescence.
Would a correct certificate check make quiescence unnecessary?

No. A certificate can establish a structural conclusion without showing that every reachability consequence has finished propagating. Conversely, settled propagation does not establish that the structural conclusion it relied on was valid. The proposal places both checks before publication.
What does ‘affected-SCC’ limit in the validation step?

It focuses certificate validation on SCCs whose structural conclusions could matter after the epoch’s changes, rather than stating that every SCC is validated from scratch. But ‘affected’ needs a sound definition: excluding an SCC whose certificate could be invalid would undermine the check. The proposal provides no size bound or algorithm for finding the affected set.
If an affected certificate does not validate, does that prove its SCC has split?

No. A certificate failing validation means its conclusion cannot be relied on as stated for that epoch. It does not, by itself, determine the resulting SCC partition. The proposed publication boundary would require resolving the structural and reachability implications before exposing the epoch, but this node does not prescribe the resolution method.
Could a concurrent insertion and deletion belong to the same sealed epoch?

The proposal does not set a batching rule, so it does not say whether any particular concurrent operations share an epoch. If both do, the sealed edge set reflects their combined result. Certificate validation and the published reachability must concern that graph, not an intermediate version containing only one of the changes.
Would validating SCC certificates against the sealed edge set settle every reachability answer?

Not by itself. SCC certificates concern structural conclusions about strong connectivity. Reachability can also depend on paths between components and on alternative routes. Before publication, the derived result for the sealed graph must be complete and match the query’s least fixed point; certificate validation is one part of establishing that, not a substitute for maintaining the whole result.
Why must atomic MVCC publication come last?

It is the point where a candidate becomes a readable committed version. Publishing earlier could expose edges from the sealed epoch paired with unfinished reachability or unchecked affected-SCC conclusions. Placing publication after quiescence and validation is intended to make the graph and derived result visible together, although atomic publication alone cannot correct a wrong result.
Can readers still use a committed epoch while the next epoch is awaiting validation?

That is consistent with MVCC snapshot reads: a reader can remain on a coherent committed version without seeing the candidate’s intermediate state. The proposal does not specify reader selection or version retention. Its publication rule concerns when the new epoch may be presented as committed.
What if a worker crashes after the edge epoch is sealed but before certificate validation finishes?

The crash must not turn the unfinished candidate into a published answer. Does this proposal guarantee that repair stays small or that updates finish within a particular time?

I’d like to explore another approach: shard source-rooted reachability forests with WAL-replayed epochs, and repair deletion-invalidated branches through surviving alternate edges before atomic MVCC publication. How would those parts fit together?

The forests would organize evidence of reachability from each source, distributed across shards. When a deletion invalidates a branch of that evidence, repair would look for alternate edges that still establish the affected reachability in the candidate epoch’s graph. WAL-replayed epochs provide a basis for retaining or recovering epoch work, and atomic MVCC publication would expose the graph and repaired result as one coherent snapshot. This is a proposal, not an implementation or a correctness result.
What does ‘source-rooted’ mean here?

It means the reachability evidence is organized around a source vertex: a rooted structure records how that source can reach other vertices. The proposal does not specify whether there is a materialized forest for every source, how roots are assigned to shards, or the representation of an individual branch.
Why call them forests if the graph can have cycles?

A forest can be a way of representing selected evidence of reachability without reproducing every edge of the cyclic graph in the evidence structure. The underlying graph may still contain cycles and multiple paths. The representation must not confuse a selected branch with the only possible route to a vertex; surviving alternate edges are important precisely because the graph can offer other routes.
Does one forest branch prove that its represented destination is reachable?

It can serve as evidence if the branch corresponds to a valid path in the epoch’s graph. But the proposal does not define the precise witness format or its validation rules. The committed answer must represent actual reachability, not merely the presence of a branch record that has become stale after an update.
How does sharding affect a source-rooted forest?

It distributes the forest’s maintenance or stored evidence across workers or partitions. A path and its potential replacements may cross shard boundaries, so a shard-local decision that a branch is lost need not settle the source’s reachability result. The proposal does not specify shard ownership, communication, or how forests are partitioned.
What is a deletion-invalidated branch?

It is a branch whose evidence can no longer be used as before because a deleted edge affects the path it represents. Invalidation of that branch does not automatically mean its destination is unreachable. Repair must determine whether another route exists in the graph version being prepared.
If an edge is deleted but no forest branch uses it, does that mean no work is needed?

The absence of that edge from a particular forest branch would mean that branch is not directly invalidated by the deletion. It does not, by itself, prove that no maintained result or other forest is affected. The proposal does not give a complete rule for locating all consequences of an edge deletion.
What counts as a surviving alternate edge?

It is an edge present in the candidate epoch’s graph that can contribute to a replacement route for reachability whose recorded branch was invalidated. Its presence alone is not sufficient: there must be a valid route from the source to its relevant endpoint and onward to the destination. The proposal does not specify a search procedure for finding or validating such routes.
So finding a different edge near the deleted one isn’t automatically enough?

Correct. A replacement must establish the required path in the updated graph. An edge might be nearby yet have no usable connection from the source, or its apparent supporting path might itself rely on deleted evidence. Repair cannot declare a result preserved solely because another edge exists.
Could an alternate route pass through another shard?

Yes. Sharding cannot limit the semantic search to the shard holding the deleted edge. If a surviving path crosses shards, the final reachability result must retain it. The proposal leaves open how the distributed repair discovers and checks that path.
What if the alternate route uses a cycle?

A cycle of surviving graph edges can form part of a genuine route. Repair should preserve reachability that the route actually establishes. It must not, however, accept forest branches that merely cite each other in a circle after their grounding paths have disappeared. The final answer is determined by the candidate graph’s least-fixed-point reachability.
Could a deletion invalidate a branch without breaking any cycle?

Yes. Branch invalidation concerns the selected evidence used by a forest, whereas breaking a graph cycle concerns the graph’s structure. Either way, an alternate route may preserve reachability, or its absence may require removing a result. The proposal cannot infer the final answer solely from whether a cycle broke.
If a cycle does break, can all vertices below the branch simply be marked unreachable?

No. Different destinations may retain different alternate paths, possibly through other parts of the graph. The invalidated branch identifies where repair should begin, not a set of results that can be removed without checking. Every committed result still has to agree with reachability in the updated graph.
What would repairing an invalidated branch involve conceptually?

Determine which source-to-destination claims depended on that branch’s evidence, check whether surviving alternate edges establish replacement routes for them, and update the forest evidence and visible reachability accordingly. That describes the obligation, not a prescribed traversal algorithm or an assertion that repair is always confined to a small subtree.
Could replacement of one branch affect several source-rooted forests?

Potentially. An edge can participate in reachability from more than one source, and evidence organized by source may therefore require work in more than one forest. The proposal does not specify how many forests are maintained or a bound on the work caused by one update.
Does the proposal also cover insertions?

The engine must still represent any new reachability that insertions create, including paths that interact with cycles. This proposal specifically describes repairing deletion-invalidated branches through surviving alternate edges; it does not supply a separate insertion-maintenance algorithm. A committed epoch containing insertions must nevertheless report reachability for the graph that includes them.
Suppose an insertion supplies an alternate route in the same epoch as a deletion. Should repair use it?

If both updates belong to the candidate epoch, its final reachability must reflect the graph containing both. The inserted edge may contribute to a valid replacement path, but neither the deletion alone nor the insertion alone determines the complete answer. The proposal does not specify how concurrent updates are grouped or ordered within epochs.
Why attach the forests to WAL-replayed epochs?

The epoch gives the graph and its derived forest evidence a version to which they can both refer. WAL replay provides a proposed durable basis for recovering epoch-related work after an interruption. The proposal does not define what forest state is logged, the replay order, or how interrupted repair is resumed; those details would have to keep recovered committed results consistent with their graph versions.
If WAL replay restores a branch that a deletion invalidated, is that branch safe to publish?

Not merely because it was replayed. Restoring a record does not prove its path still exists in the graph of the epoch being published. Any invalidated evidence must be repaired or replaced, and any reachability it supports must be correct for that epoch, before publication.
What if a worker crashes midway through searching for alternate edges?

Unfinished search must not be mistaken for proof that the branch has a replacement or that no replacement exists. The candidate epoch must remain unpublished as a complete answer until necessary repair has been accounted for. WAL replay is named in the proposal, but the exact recovery and completion protocol is not specified.
Where does atomic MVCC publication enter?

It is the visibility boundary after the relevant updates and branch repairs have produced a coherent candidate result. A reader pinned to a committed epoch should not see new edges combined with old, invalidated forest evidence, or a provisional answer awaiting alternate-route checks. Atomicity prevents a partially prepared combination from being exposed as one snapshot; it cannot make incorrect repair correct.
Can readers stay on an older epoch during repair?

That is consistent with MVCC snapshot reading: a previously committed epoch can provide a coherent view while the next candidate is being repaired. The proposal does not prescribe reader selection or how long older versions are retained.
What has to be true of a repaired forest before the new epoch is published?

Its evidence must not justify results through paths absent from that epoch’s graph, and the visible reachability answer must not omit results supported by surviving routes. More broadly, the published answer must equal least-fixed-point recomputation for the same graph version. The proposal does not supply a proof that a particular forest representation meets those obligations.
Does ‘repair deletion-invalidated branches’ guarantee repair stays local?

No. A branch gives a starting point for affected work, but a replacement path could run through other shards, and a deletion could affect reachability from multiple sources. The proposal gives no touched-vertex bound, latency threshold, or guarantee that each repair region is small.
Would examining a broad region turn the method into full-query recomputation?

Not necessarily. Targeted repair can be broad for a consequential deletion without being an unconditional full-query recomputation after each individual update. The proposal is to maintain branch evidence incrementally and seek surviving alternate routes, but it does not measure update work or establish a formal complexity bound.
Can you give me a concise description that remains clearly a proposal?

“Propose sharding source-rooted reachability forests across WAL-replayed epochs, repairing branches invalidated by deletions through valid surviving alternate edges, and atomically publishing each complete MVCC snapshot.” This describes the approach without claiming an implementation, a small repair region, or a verified correctness outcome.

What does ‘versioned’ mean for a source-rooted forest?

A forest can organize selected evidence of paths from a source without claiming that the underlying graph is acyclic. The graph can have cycles and multiple routes to the same vertex. If a selected branch becomes invalid, the existence of another route must be checked rather than inferred from the old forest’s shape.

It is a part of the maintained forest whose path evidence is no longer reliable after an update, particularly a deletion. Invalidation of the evidence does not establish that the destination has become unreachable: another path might still support it. It supplies a prospective starting point whose reachability evidence remains valid for the candidate graph version. Could the frontier be on a different shard from the invalidated branch?

The plan does not prescribe placement. In a distributed reachability engine, valid paths can cross shard boundaries, so a repair cannot assume that a replacement route must be local to the deleted edge or branch. How shards discover and coordinate a reattachment remains unspecified.
Is finding any alternate edge sufficient to reattach a branch?

No. An alternate edge must participate in a path from the source through an intact frontier to the part being reattached, using edges present in the candidate graph. An edge whose purported source-side support also depends on the invalidated branch would not, merely by being different, establish a valid replacement.
Could two invalidated branches reattach through each other?

Not if their only justification is circular dependence on evidence already invalidated. A reattachment has to be grounded in a surviving route from the source through valid graph edges. The maintained result must retain those vertices’ reachability where the alternate route actually exists and remove results for which no route remains. And if the deletion leaves the cycle intact?

The resulting graph still determines the answer. An intact cycle may preserve some reachability, but it does not prove that every connection affected by the deleted edge survives. Does reattaching an invalidated branch guarantee that everything beneath it is reachable?

Only if the replacement path and the remaining branch paths are valid in the candidate version. Some downstream evidence might also have been invalidated. The plan does not say that one reattachment automatically validates every descendant; that would have to be established before relying on it in a committed answer.
Could a deletion affect forests rooted at more than one source?

Yes, an edge can contribute to paths from multiple sources. The plan does not promise that one deletion affects just one forest or a small number of branches. All reachability consequences of the candidate epoch still have to be accounted for before publication.
Is ‘intact’ something we can determine from the old forest alone?

Not necessarily. A frontier that was valid in an earlier version might depend on an edge deleted in the candidate version or on another invalidated branch. Its status has to be justified for the version in which it is used. The plan names intact frontiers but leaves their validity test open.
How do concurrent insertions fit with a deletion-based reattachment plan?

If an insertion belongs to the same candidate epoch, it may create a new route that affects whether a branch can be reattached or which results are reachable. The committed answer must reflect all updates in that epoch. This plan focuses on reattaching deletion-invalidated branches and does not provide a separate insertion-maintenance procedure or batching rule.
Could repair use a path that existed only before the epoch’s deletion?

What is meant by sealing WAL/MVCC epochs?

The plan calls for an epoch boundary that ties durable WAL-backed work to a coherent MVCC version for readers. Sealing should distinguish a completed version from a candidate whose forest repair is still underway. The wording does not specify a WAL record format, distributed sealing protocol, or precise recovery sequence.

An epoch must not be exposed as a complete committed answer merely because work associated with it has been logged.

MVCC provides a way to read a coherent committed version while a candidate epoch is being prepared. A reader must not see new graph edges paired with forest evidence that has not been repaired for that version. The plan does not specify reader-pinning mechanics or retention of older epochs.

An unfinished search must not be interpreted as proof that an alternate path exists or does not exist.
